title: Building detail of Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan
caption: A master class in pattern
subtitle: Building detail of Registan Square, Samarkand, Uzbekistan
description:
Stand in Registan Square and it's easy to see why it is considered the architectural heart of Samarkand—one of Central Asia's oldest cities. This plaza in Uzbekistan is framed by three magnificent madrasas—Islamic centres of learning—whose soaring portals draw the eye upwards. Yet some of the square's greatest treasures reveal themselves only when you look closer.
The detail in today's image offers a glimpse of the artistry that covers nearly every surface. Glazed tiles, geometric motifs, floral designs and elegant calligraphy come together with remarkable precision, turning brick and plaster into a dazzling display of colour and pattern. Shades of turquoise, cobalt, gold and white shift with the changing light, giving the architecture a sense of movement throughout the day.
Built as centres of learning and religious scholarship, the madrasas surrounded a lively public square that was once a focal point of life along the Silk Road. Today, Registan remains just as captivating, inviting visitors to admire both its monumental scale and its extraordinary craftsmanship.

title: Horsehair parachute fungus, Belarus
caption: A world beneath your feet
subtitle: Horsehair parachute fungus, Belarus
description:
Tiny mushrooms often go unnoticed, but the horsehair parachute fungus deserves a closer look. With a stem as thin as a strand of horsehair and a pleated cap measuring just 0.5 to 1 centimetre across, this miniature mushroom proves that good things really do come in small packages.
Its wiry black stem is surprisingly tough, helping it stay upright on rotting twigs and dead wood across damp forests. While it isn't poisonous, it's far too small and tough to end up on anyone's plate.
The fungus has another clever trick up its cap. Unlike many mushrooms that release spores on an internal daily schedule, it waits for rainfall before launching them into the air, making wet weather the perfect time to spread. As it breaks down dead plant material, it helps recycle nutrients and enrich forest soils. Some closely related horsehair fungi even weave thread-like hyphae that catch falling leaves before they land. It's living proof that, in the fungal world, the smallest players often make the biggest contribution.

title: Traditional beach huts, Southwold, Suffolk Heritage Coast, England
caption: Painted along the shore
subtitle: Beach huts, Southwold, Suffolk Heritage Coast, England
description:
Along England's east coast, the Suffolk Heritage Coast blends windswept heaths, marshes, shingle beaches and expansive North Sea views. One of its best-known towns is Southwold, where water and history are inseparable. Almost encircled by the sea, the River Blyth and surrounding wetlands, the town occupies a slender peninsula shaped by centuries of fishing, trade and life at the edge of the water.
The colourful wooden beach huts are among Southwold's most recognisable landmarks. Originally built as simple bathing and fishing shelters, today hundreds line the shore, adding bright bands of colour against the sand and sky. Some remain treasured family possessions, passed down through generations.
Beyond the huts, visitors find a working lighthouse, a pier stretching into the North Sea and easy access to coastal paths that reveal some of England's most celebrated scenery. It's a shoreline that rewards wandering—one where every bend seems to open onto another story of the sea.

title: Coyote Buttes, Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, Arizona, United States
caption: An act of wilderness
subtitle: Coyote Buttes, Arizona, United States
description:
Waves usually belong to the ocean. In northern Arizona, United States, they rise from the desert instead. The swirling sandstone formations of Coyote Buttes, part of Vermilion Cliffs National Monument, were shaped by ancient dunes and millions of years of erosion, creating a landscape that seems to ripple even while standing still.
Places like this are one reason the Wilderness Act of 1964 was signed into law on 3 September, a milestone commemorated today. Concerned that an expanding nation could transform nearly every corner of the country, Congress established the National Wilderness Preservation System to protect lands that retain their natural character and offer opportunities for solitude, exploration and discovery.
The act initially safeguarded 54 wilderness areas covering 9.1 million acres (3.68 million hectares). More than six decades later, the system now encompasses over 110 million acres (44.5 million hectares) nationwide. From remote forests to sculpted desert rock, these protected landscapes invite visitors to experience a side of America shaped not by blueprints, but by time itself.

title: Westerheversand Lighthouse in Westerhever, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
caption: Red and white on the horizon
subtitle: Westerheversand Lighthouse, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany
description:
Rising above the salt marshes along Germany's North Sea coast, Westerheversand Lighthouse is instantly recognisable for its distinctive red-and-white stripes. Built between 1906 and 1908 on 127 heavy wooden piles driven into the sand, the 40-metre cast-iron tower has stood on the Eiderstedt Peninsula for more than a century, guiding ships through the North Sea. Two identical white keeper's cottages flank the beacon, adding to its storybook appearance.
The lighthouse stands within Schleswig-Holstein Wadden Sea National Park, part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Wadden Sea. Reached by a 2.5-kilometre trail across the salt marshes, it offers sweeping views of tidal flats and a landscape constantly reshaped by the ebb and flow of the sea. Visitors can climb its 157 steps, while one of the former keeper's cottages now serves as a registry office for weddings.
Automated in 1978, the lighthouse no longer needs resident keepers, but it remains a striking symbol of Germany's North Sea coast and its ever-changing tidal landscape.

title: California sea lions hunting a sardine bait ball, offshore Mexico, Pacific Ocean
caption: Masters of the surf and shore
subtitle: California sea lions, offshore Mexico, Pacific Ocean
description:
A day at the beach is rarely quiet when California sea lions are around. With their booming barks, playful personalities and a knack for stealing the spotlight, these marine mammals know how to put on a show.
Found along the Pacific coast from British Columbia to Mexico, California sea lions are among the few animals that seem just as comfortable on land as they are in the water. Adult males are easy to spot thanks to the distinctive forehead bump, or sagittal crest. Unlike true seals, they rotate their hind flippers forward, allowing them to 'walk' or even run on all fours. In the ocean, they power through the water with their large front flippers, reaching speeds of up to 25 mph. They're also famous for jugging—floating upright with their flippers raised above the surface to help regulate their body temperature.
Whether lounging on shore or gliding through the waves, California sea lions are among the most charismatic animals along the Pacific coast.

title: Lake Fyans, Grampians National Park, Victoria, Australia
caption: A reservoir of reflections
subtitle: Lake Fyans, Grampians National Park, Victoria, Australia
description:
At first glance, today's image looks more like a drowned woodland than a lake. Bare tree trunks emerge from the water, their reflections stretching across the surface as the Grampians glow in the distance. This is Lake Fyans, a man-made off-stream reservoir at the foot of the Grampians (Gariwerd) National Park in Victoria, Australia. Part of the regional Wimmera-Mallee water supply system, it also draws anglers with its brown and rainbow trout and trophy-sized redfin.
The mountains beyond the lake are part of the Grampians, a range shaped over hundreds of millions of years. Today, the region is known for rugged sandstone peaks, dramatic lookouts, waterfalls and rich Aboriginal cultural heritage. On the water, visitors can sail, kayak, jet-ski and water-ski, while trails through the surrounding landscape offer encounters with kangaroos, emus and native birds.
Lake Fyans captures that wild spirit in a single scene: flooded trees, open skies and an ever-changing backdrop of ancient mountains.

title: Old Town Hall, Bamberg, Germany
caption: Where history flows along the canal
description: Perched above the Regnitz River, Bamberg's Old Town Hall is one of Germany's most distinctive landmarks. According to local legend, the town's bishop refused to give citizens land for their town hall, so they created their own artificial island in the river by driving wooden piles into the riverbed. The building that rose there became a symbol of civic independence and remains one of Bavaria's most photographed scenes.
